To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
The nucleotide sequence preceding the tryptophon operon genes of E. coli has been established.

the nucleotide sequence of the 1179 bp intercistronic DNA region preceding the trp operons genes has been established and that there are no open reading frame large enough to code proteins containing more than about 100 amino acids.

the DNA region preceding the trp operons is not a promoter but an intercistron, that the trp genes are preceded by a 1179 base pair long intercistronic sequence, and that this sequence does not contain any open reading frame that is large enough to encode proteins containing more than about 100 amino acid residues.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the primary structure of the DNA region preceding the genes of the E. colitryptophan operon (trpEDCBA).
the study of the regulation of the tryptophane operon.
the study of the regulation of the expression of the tryptophane operon in E. coli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the intercistronic DNA region preceding the E. coli trp operon genes is a typical prokaryotic DNA region.
this DNA segment is devoid of genes and therefore represents the intercistronic sequence between the trp operon and the adjacent gene coding for a 5.8S RNA molecule.
this region is not coding for any protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the E. coli trp operon genes are not organized in a polycistronic operon but in a series of monocistronic units.
the DNA sequence of the trp promoter and operator regions is not unique in E. coli, but that the sequence preceding the trp operons is unique in the genome.
the trp genes and their control elements are located on a single operon, the transcription of which is initiated from a single promoter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the intercistronic regions preceding trp genes are highly conserved in E. coli and Salmonella typhimurium.
we have identified a novel protein in the brain that is expressed in neurons and is associated with the synapse.
the DNA region preceding trp operon genes does not contain any regulatory elements.
